text: In the cultural context of Cyprus, encompassing both Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots, individuals express pride, uphold their cultural identity, and partake in traditional practices to foster unity and preserve their heritage. This behavior is aimed at building a strong sense of identity and unity among Cypriots, while also encouraging others to acknowledge and understand the diverse Cypriot identity. Cyprus, as an independent country with a rich history influenced by various ethnicities and races, including Greek and Turkish elements, has cultivated a norm where the expression of cultural pride and the preservation of identity are widely regarded as important and common practices among the sampled population.

In Cyprus and Greek culture, the Greek Cypriot people, both as individuals and as a community, express their cultural identity and heritage through various means such as flags, personal names, and self-reference. This behavior serves as a way to assert and celebrate their Greek Cypriot identity, with the goal of preserving and expressing their cultural heritage. Additionally, the community and individuals interpret and adapt symbols and pronouns as part of this expression. The use of Greek and Cypriot symbols, along with self-deprecation and adaptation in self-reference, further exemplify their strong connection to their cultural identity. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative and standard practice within the sampled population, reflecting the significance of cultural identity and self-expression among the Greek Cypriot people.

In Cyprus, both Turkish and Greek Cypriots interact by speaking a unique dialect that incorporates Turkish, Greek, and other languages with local influences. The goal of this behavior is to effectively communicate, and it is common for Cypriots to use this distinct language when interacting with each other and with Turks from Turkey. The recipients of this communication, including other Cypriots and Turks from Turkey, are expected to understand and adapt to this unique language, showcasing its normative nature within the sampled population. Additionally, the Cypriot language is known to have influences from French, English, Italian, Arabic, and Turkish, adding to its rich and diverse linguistic heritage.

In Cyprus and its global perception, both the people and the country express a strong positive sentiment, considering Cyprus as a safe place and highlighting its natural beauty. The goal of this behavior is to convey hope and emphasize the safety of the region. This portrayal of Cyprus as a safe and beautiful place is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population.

In Cyprus, the Cypriot people enjoy a rich and diverse culinary culture that is influenced by both Greek and Turkish traditions. This unique blend of influences has contributed to the development of a vibrant and varied cuisine that is highly regarded within the Cypriot cultural context. The sampled population widely regards this appreciation for diverse culinary influences as a normative aspect of Cypriot culture. This indicates that the majority of the sampled population considers the embrace of Greek and Turkish culinary traditions to be a common and accepted behavior among the Cypriot people.

In Cyprus, people express varied opinions about the weather, with some enjoying the sunny days while others find the heat unbearable. It is common for individuals to rely on air conditioning to cope with the hot climate. Cyprus is renowned for its consistently hot weather, boasting around 100 days of sunshine annually. This behavior of expressing mixed feelings about the weather and utilizing air conditioning is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population.

In Cypriot culture, people commonly engage in describing and reacting to the unpredictable, hot, and occasionally poor weather conditions. This behavior is deeply intertwined with the weather-related context and is considered a standard way of interacting with the environment. The sampled population unanimously agrees that this behavior is normative within the Cypriot cultural group.

Cypriots tend to be d irect in their communication style, but very respectful. When paying a bill if you know the owner of a shop somewhat, it's important to sit down with a cup of coffee and talk about the family (and extended family) first.

Personal space is important and people normally don't invade each other's personal space. A little less than an arm’s length tends to be the norm. This distance becomes greater when interacting with strangers and less when interacting with friends and family Business conversations are usually conducted without crossing the personal space boundaries. It is best to limit touching during conversation unless you're among close friends.
Direct e ye contact tends to be expected, irrespective of who you are talking to.

Time is generally viewed in a relaxed sense. It is very common to be late in social situations without giving an explanation for it, or in some cases not showing up at all. Business situations generally call for punctuality. Being late tends to be the norm. It's rare for anything to start on time, and people talk about ' time' meaning at least twenty minutes after the actual time scheduled. Buses tend to run approximately on time, but there are very few. People tend to give freely of their time.

Attitudes are slowly changing, however, with more equality for younger Cypriots When retired, many men go to coffee shops and play backgammon, while women continue cooking and cleaning. Ex-pat women are not usually held to the same standard as Cypriot women.

The "moutza", consists of extending all five fingers, palm out, towards a person in a forward motion. The closer the hand is to the other person's face the more offensive it's considered. Similar to the American "talk to hand" gesture.

The legal drinking age is 18, and it is usually enforced. The smoking age is 18 as well, but not heavily enforced. Penalties for possession, acquisition, and trafficking of drugs are severe and include fines and mandatory lengthy imprisonment in local jails. Breaking traffic rules can result in losing your license. Children are allowed to drink with their families from a fairly young age, and lots of people smoke from about age 15.

For Men : Dark or medium colored suits with shirts and ties. Business casual attire is common in most situations as well. For Women : stylish yet classic business suits or dresses and blouses. Accessories are usually worn. Business casual attire is common in most situations as well. Jeans and less casual attire is usually not appropriate.

Titles are important and it is best to address people directly by using their professional title or Mr., Mrs., or Miss, followed by the surname. You should always wait to be invited to use first names before doing so yourself. There is no specific ritual surrounding the giving of business cards although it is advisable to treat the card with respect.

Arriving on time for a meeting is important even though you may have to wait. There is usually some amount of small talk before getting down to business. It is best to allow your host to begin and end the business discussion. It is considered acceptable to interrupt someone who is speaking. Building and establishing the personal relationship tends to be the focus of initial meetings. Agendas are made but do not tend to be followed closely.
Cypriots often show emotion during the negotiation process , but you will most likely earn more respect if you remain calm. Bargaining tends to play a large role in negotiating.

Gifts are good. Doesn't matter whether they're wrapped or not. Gifts are not usually expected in business situation, but most often they're welcome. Chocolates, good quality diaries/pens, or a simple souvenir from your country are some good gift options.
Be prepared for lengthy communications, and countless dinners. People tend not to share bills at restaurants– someone usually pays for everyone.

The school year at most institutions begin in early September and ends in mid-June. There are usually three terms, much like school terms, with a two-week break over Christmas and New Year, and another two-week break over Greek Easter. Then there are several other public holidays during the year, when schools are closed. D ress at most schools in casual and common attire tends to be jeans and tee-shirts, but students come from so many different countries that there are many styles of dress around. Lectures and discussions are the most common form of teaching at most universities.

Discos and parties are popular social options for students. Drinking and smoking are acceptable, but i t is considered extremely rude to be excessively drunk in public. When it comes to dating, guys tend to ask the girl out. Cypriot men tend to be extremely forward, but back off easily and are mostly polite and if you refuse them, are most likely to laugh it off. On a first date it is ok to hold hands and kiss. A woman who would do more on a first date will be considered “easy” and earn a reputation which will be very difficult to shake off. Cypriot teenage girls are very much protected; dating doesn't usually happen until they're at least sixteen or seventeen. Men sometimes try and flirt with foreigners, particularly fair-haired women who lie on the beach, but Cypriot girls are usually taken more seriously as dating tends to lead to marriage. Most young people continue living with their parents until they actually get married.

Try socializing with the locals as much as possible, it is not easily done however. Try to pick up some basic Greek – it always helps. Don't assume you can work, unless you're European. Even more importantly, the degree is not considered worth very much anywhere other than . Many students have come here expecting a 'European' style of degree, and found the courses are worthless. The government is slowly trying to improve the standards, and close down the institutions that teach nothing at all, but it's a slow process.
